entities.name: Theodotus of Byzantium
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Theodotus of Byzantium, a leather-worker (or shoemaker) turned theologian, emerged in the late 2nd century CE in Rome, having migrated from Byzantium. He is primarily known as the founder of Theodotianism, a form of dynamic monarchianism or adoptionism, which asserted that Jesus was merely a man, born of a virgin, upon whom the Christ descended at his baptism, making him divine by adoption rather than inherent nature. His teachings represented a significant challenge to the developing orthodox Christology, particularly in the Roman church under Popes Victor I and Zephyrinus, as early Christian communities grappled with defining the nature of Christ in relation to God the Father.

Theodotus arrived in Rome around 190 CE, where he began to propagate his unique interpretation of Christ's divinity. He taught that Jesus was a righteous man chosen by God, empowered by the Holy Spirit at his baptism, but not divine in essence before this event. This doctrine directly countered emerging Trinitarian views and was swiftly condemned as heresy by Pope Victor I, leading to Theodotus's excommunication from the Roman church. Despite this, his followers formed a distinct sect, including a later Theodotus (the banker) and Artemon, who continued to promote adoptionist views and even established their own bishop, Natalius, for a time.

The legacy of Theodotus of Byzantium lies in his role as a catalyst for the precise definition of orthodox Christology. His radical humanization of Christ forced early Church Fathers, such as Tertullian and Hippolytus, to articulate more clearly the dual nature of Christ—fully human and fully divine—and the concept of the Trinity. The condemnation of Theodotianism underscored the Roman Church's growing authority in theological matters and set a precedent for identifying and suppressing doctrines deemed heterodox, shaping the future trajectory of Christian dogma and ecclesiastical power structures.
